<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/05-setup/first-moves/ -->

# Calibrate, activate, move

Every session with the gripper starts the same way: calibrate, activate, clear what errors there are. Then it
moves. This page does it once with Motor GUI, with Python and over UART; [How the gripper works](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/how-it-works/)
explains what happens inside.

!!! danger
    The jaws move over the whole stroke during calibration, and close with the set force afterwards. Nothing in
    reach of them, fingers included.

## 1. Power up

At power-up the gripper reports *Not calibrated* and does not move. Its stepper must be calibrated too, which a
bought gripper is from the factory; a self-built gripper gets that in [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/first-run/).

## 2. Calibrate

The gripper calibration finds the two end stops: the jaws open fully, pause, then close fully, at low force
(500 mA) and low speed. Each end is recognised when the jaws have stood still against it for half a second. It
takes about ten seconds; the result is not kept over a power cycle, so this runs at every power-up.

=== "Motor GUI"
    **Calibrate**, and confirm. When the jaws stop, the panel shows *Calibrated*.

=== "Python"
    ```python
    gripper.Send_gripper_calibrate()
    time.sleep(10)
    ```

=== "UART"
    ```
    #Gripcal
    ```

If the jaws do not move at all, or move to one end and stop: the gripper is in an error state (clear it first, see
step 4), or the stepper is not calibrated. If the routine runs for 24 seconds and gives up, an end stop was not
found: something blocks the jaws short of the end, or the mechanism is too stiff for 500 mA.

## 3. Activate

A calibrated gripper carries out a move only while it is activated.

=== "Motor GUI"
    **Activate**. The panel shows *Activated*.

=== "Python"
    The activate bit is part of every move command, its fourth argument; send it as 1. To activate without
    moving, send a command with the action bit, the fifth argument, at 0:

    ```python
    gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(0, 30, 300, 1, 0, 0, 0)   # position, speed, current, activate = 1, action = 0, E-stop, release direction
    ```

=== "UART"
    `#Grippos` activates by itself; `#Gripact 1` activates without moving.

## 4. Clear errors

The driver powers up in an error state until its motor is calibrated and it has run through its checks; an
E-stop, an over-temperature or a supply fault leave an error too. A gripper with an error does not move.

=== "Motor GUI"
    **Clear errors**, when the panel shows an error.

=== "Python"
    ```python
    gripper.Send_Clear_Error()
    ```

=== "UART"
    ```
    #Clear
    ```

An error whose cause is still present comes straight back; [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/errors/) says
what each needs.

## 5. Move

A move is three numbers: the position (0 open, 255 closed), the speed (0 to 255: linear from 1.6 to 190 mm/s at
each jaw) and the current limit in mA, which is the grip force ([Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/)).
Start with speed 30, about 24 mm/s at each jaw, and 300 mA.

=== "Motor GUI"
    Set *Speed* 30 and *Current* 300 with their **Set** buttons, then **Close** and **Open**, or set a *Position*:
    the jaws follow, the plots show the position and the current, and the state says whether the jaws reached
    the position or stopped on something.

=== "Python"
    ```python
    gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(200, 30, 300, 1, 1, 0, 0)   # position, speed, current, activate, action, E-stop, release direction
    time.sleep(2)
    gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(20, 30, 300, 1, 1, 0, 0)
    ```

=== "UART"
    ```
    #Gripvel 30
    #Gripcur 300
    #Grippos 200
    #Grippos 20
    ```

Put an object between the jaws and close on it: the jaws stop on it and hold it with 300 mA, and the state reads
*object detected while closing*. Raise the current for a firmer grip, within the stepper's rating, and the speed
once the motion is what you want.

## What the gripper reports

Every move command is answered with the gripper's state, which Motor GUI shows in its panel and the
library puts into attributes: the position, the current, whether it is calibrated and activated, whether a move
is in progress, the object-detection result, and the three error bits. [How the gripper works](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/how-it-works/)
goes through them.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/ -->

# Operation

How a working gripper is used: what happens inside when it calibrates and moves, the interfaces it is driven
through, and what to do when it reports an error.

## In this chapter

- [How the gripper works](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/how-it-works/)
- [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/can/)
- [Over UART](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/uart/)
- [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/python/)
- [With ROS 2](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/ros2/)
- [On PAROL6 and PAR6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/robots/)
- [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/errors/)

The exact layout of every message and command is in the [API reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/how-it-works/ -->

# How the gripper works

The gripper is a state machine in the driver's firmware, fed by one command and answering with one status. This
page is what it does with them.

## The states

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NotCalibrated: power-up
    NotCalibrated --> Calibrating: Send_gripper_calibrate / #Gripcal
    Calibrating --> Calibrated: both end stops found
    Calibrating --> NotCalibrated: 24 s without an end stop
    Calibrated --> Moving: command with activate = 1, action = 1
    Moving --> Holding: object found, or position reached
    Holding --> Moving: a different command
    Moving --> Idle: error, E-stop, action = 0
    Holding --> Idle: error, E-stop, action = 0
    Idle --> Moving: command, errors cleared
```

**Not calibrated**

- After power-up the gripper does not know where its jaws are.
- It answers status requests and refuses moves.
- The gripper calibration is not kept over a power cycle.

**Calibrating**

- The jaws open at speed 40 and 500 mA until they have stood still against the end stop for half a second.
- They pause briefly, then close the same way.
- The two end positions become 0 (open) and 255 (closed).
- If an end stop is not found within 24 seconds, the routine gives up and the gripper stays uncalibrated.
- Nothing else is accepted while it runs; the action bit of the status reads 0.

**Moving**

- A command with the activate and action bits set starts a move towards the position, at the speed.
- The current is limited to the commanded value.
- The driver runs its velocity loop towards the target and watches two things: the speed of the jaws and the
  motor current.

**Holding**: the move ends in one of two ways.

- **Position reached** (within 5 encoder ticks): the driver switches to position control and holds the jaws
  there. Object detection reads 3.
- **Object in the way**: the jaws stop before the target with the current at its limit. The driver keeps pushing
  with the limited current, which is the grip. Object detection reads 1 if the jaws were closing, 2 if they were
  opening.
- Either way, nothing moves until a different command arrives.

**Idle**

- An error, the E-stop bit, or a command with the action bit at 0 takes the gripper to idle.
- The motor is no longer driven and holds nothing beyond the mechanism's friction, so an object can slip.
- Clearing the error, or the next command with the action bit set, moves it again.

## The command

Send_gripper_data_pack carries, in 5 bytes:

| Field | Range | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Position | 0 to 255 | 0 fully open, 255 fully closed, linear over the stroke |
| Speed | 0 to 255 | 1.6 to 190 mm/s at each jaw, linear (500 to 60000 encoder ticks per second); see [Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/) |
| Current | mA | the current limit of the move, so the grip force; not clamped by the firmware |
| Activate | bit | 1 activates the gripper; 0 deactivates it, and it stops |
| Action | bit | 1 carries out the move; 0 stores the command and leaves the gripper idle |
| E-stop | bit | 1 stops the gripper and raises the E-stop error |
| Release direction | bit | read by the firmware but not used |

The same command sent twice does nothing new: the driver compares every command with the previous one, and only
a changed command resets the "at position" state and starts a move. So a host may repeat the command at any
rate, which the CAN watchdog needs; to move the jaws from a held position to the same position again, change
the speed or the current by one.

An empty Send_gripper_data_pack, 0 bytes, changes nothing and is answered like a full one: it is the status poll,
and it costs the bus almost nothing. A host usually sends one full command per move and polls with empty ones.

Over UART, `#Grippos` is the same command: it sets the position, activates the gripper, sets the action bit and
starts the move, with the speed and current last set by `#Gripvel` and `#Gripcur` (50 and 400 mA after power-up).

## The answer

Every Send_gripper_data_pack is answered with Respond_Gripper_data_pack, 4 bytes:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Position | where the jaws are, 0 to 255 |
| Current | the motor current, mA; positive while opening, negative while closing |
| Activated | the activate flag |
| Action status | 1 while a move is in progress, 0 when idle, holding, or calibrating |
| Object detection | 0 moving, 1 object found while closing, 2 object found while opening, 3 at the position |
| Temperature error | the motor's thermistor is above the limit |
| Timeout error | the driver's CAN watchdog ran out |
| E-stop error | the E-stop bit was received |
| Calibrated | the gripper calibration is done |

The bits are listed in [Errors and status bits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/errors/), with the byte layout in the
[CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/gripper/).

## A grip, message by message

What a host sends and what comes back, from power-up to a held object:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant G as Gripper
    H->>G: Send_Clear_Error
    H->>G: Send_gripper_calibrate
    G-->>H: status: calibrating (action status 0)
    Note over G: the jaws open, pause, close: 0 and 255 are found
    G-->>H: status: calibrated
    H->>G: Send_gripper_data_pack(200, 30, 400, activate 1, action 1)
    G-->>H: answer: moving (object detection 0)
    loop every 20 ms, an empty Send_gripper_data_pack
        H->>G: (0 bytes)
        G-->>H: answer: position, current, state
    end
    G-->>H: answer: object found while closing (1), or at the position (3)
    Note over H: the grip is in, the next move waits for the program
```

## Object detection, exactly

While a move is in progress and the jaws are not yet at the target, the driver reads *moving* (0) as long as the
jaws move faster than 500 encoder ticks per second, about 1.6 mm/s. When they are slower than that and the motor
current is above 80 % of the commanded limit, something stops them: *object found*, 1 or 2 by the sign of the
current. Below 80 % with the jaws slow, it still reads *moving*: the jaws are accelerating or the object is soft
and still being squeezed. Once the target is reached, 3, and it stays 3 until a different command arrives.

The state is therefore a snapshot of each answer. A host that wants to know "did the grip succeed" sends the move,
then polls until the state is 1, 2 or 3, with a timeout of its own; the ROS 2 driver and the PAROL6 software do
exactly that.

## What the current limit does

The current limit of a move is the driver's Iq limit for the duration of the move and the hold. It bounds the
torque, so the force on an object, and it also bounds how fast the jaws accelerate: a low limit with a high speed
gives a gentle, slow-starting move. The temperature of the motor is the other bound: holding an object at a high
current for minutes heats the windings, and at 75 °C the thermistor stops the gripper.

## Timing

The driver runs its loops at 6250 Hz; a move command takes effect at the next cycle, and the answer leaves within
a millisecond. The CAN bus at 1 Mbit/s carries a command and its answer in well under half a millisecond, so a host
can run the gripper at several hundred commands per second; 50 Hz is a good rate for a controller that polls the
state.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/can/ -->

# Over CAN

CAN is the gripper's interface: the one cable carries it next to the power, and a robot's control board, a PC with
the CANvas adapter or any microcontroller with a CAN transceiver drives the gripper with it. The gripper is a
STEPFOC driver on the bus, so the frames are the driver's; this page is the part a gripper needs.

## The frame

CAN 2.0 data frames with 11-bit identifiers at 1 Mbit/s. The identifier carries the node, the command and the
error state:

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The CAN identifier](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/assets/CANID.PNG){ width="600" }
  <figcaption>Figure 15: Bits 10 to 7 of the identifier are the node ID, bits 6 to 1 the command ID, bit 0 the error bit.</figcaption>
</figure>

- **Node ID**, bits 10 to 7: which device. Every gripper ships as node 0; set another with Send_CAN_ID or `#CANID`
  and save it. Use 0 to 13: the driver's bootloader reserves 14 and 15, and a device on one of those cannot be
  updated over CAN.
- **Command ID**, bits 6 to 1: which message. The gripper command is 61, its answer 60, the calibration 62.
- **Error bit**, bit 0: in a frame from the gripper, 1 while any error is active. In a frame from the host it is
  ignored.

So the gripper command to node 0 travels on identifier `(0 << 7) | (61 << 1)` = 0x7A, and the answer comes back on
`(60 << 1) | error` = 0x78 or 0x79; to node 3 the command is 0x1FA and the answer 0x1F8. Multi-byte values are
big-endian; flags inside a byte are numbered from the most significant bit.

## The messages a gripper needs

| Message | ID | What for |
|---|---|---|
| [Send_gripper_data_pack](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/gripper/#send_gripper_data_pack) | 61 | the move command: position, speed, current, the activate, action and E-stop bits; 0 bytes to poll |
| [Respond_Gripper_data_pack](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/gripper/#respond_gripper_data_pack) | 60 | the answer: position, current, the state and error bits |
| [Send_gripper_calibrate](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/gripper/#send_gripper_calibrate) | 62 | the gripper calibration, after every power-up |
| [Send_Clear_Error](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_clear_error) | 1 | clears the errors |
| [Send_ESTOP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_estop), [Send_Idle](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_idle) | 0, 12 | stop |
| [Send_Watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_watchdog) | 15 | the gripper stops when the host stops talking |
| [Send_CAN_ID](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_can_id), [Send_Save_config](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_save_config) | 11, 13 | another node ID, saved |
| [Send_Respond_State_of_Errors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/status/#send_respond_state_of_errors), [Send_Respond_Temperature](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/status/#send_respond_temperature) | 26, 23 | the driver's error flags, the motor temperature |

The [CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/) has the bytes of each; the driver's other messages, which a
gripper does not need, are on the [STEPFOC site](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/reference/can/).

## A control loop

1. At power-up: Send_Clear_Error, then Send_gripper_calibrate; poll with empty Send_gripper_data_pack frames
   until the calibrated bit is 1 (about ten seconds).
2. For each grip: one Send_gripper_data_pack with the position, speed and current and the activate and action
   bits set; then poll with empty frames until the object-detection field reads 1, 2 or 3, or your own timeout
   passes.
3. Keep polling at a steady rate (50 Hz is plenty) if you set the watchdog: every frame resets it, and the gripper
   stops by itself when your program stops.

The answer to every frame tells the whole state, so a host never has to ask twice.

## From a PC

The [CANvas adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter) shows up as a serial port and
speaks slcan; `python-can` opens it with `bustype='slcan'`, and the [Python library](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/python/) wraps the messages.
Any CAN adapter that `python-can` supports works the same way.

## On a bus with other devices

A gripper on a robot shares the bus with the robot's joints or other grippers. Give each device its own node ID
(connect one at a time, Send_CAN_ID, Send_Save_config), terminate both ends of the bus
([CAN termination](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/04-installation/can-termination/)), and keep in mind that a lower node ID wins the bus
arbitration.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/uart/ -->

# Over UART

The driver inside the gripper has a serial port. It is not the gripper's everyday interface, which is CAN, but it
is the way to configure the driver of a self-built gripper and the quickest way to look at what the driver
reports when something is wrong.

## Reaching the port

The UART connector of the driver (JST SH, 4 pins, 3.3 V) is inside the housing, under the coupler plate. Unscrew
the plate, plug in the [USB-to-serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter) with
the UART cable, and open a terminal at 256000 baud with CR+LF line endings; the gripper's 24 V must be on for
anything but reading settings. [The serial terminal](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/05-setup/terminal/)
on the STEPFOC site walks through the terminal setup.

!!! danger
    The port is 3.3 V. A 5 V adapter destroys the driver.

## The gripper commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `#Gripper 1` | gripper mode on (set and saved on every gripper); `#Gripper` prints it |
| `#Gripcal` | the gripper calibration |
| `#Gripvel 30` | the speed of the next moves, 0 to 255 |
| `#Gripcur 300` | the current limit of the next moves, mA |
| `#Grippos 200` | move to the position, 0 open to 255 closed; activates the gripper and starts the move |
| `#Gripact 1` | the activate flag without moving |
| `#Gripstop 1` | the E-stop bit |
| `#Gripinfo` | the gripper's state: calibrated, activated, the setpoints, the object detection, the end stops |

Only `#Grippos` starts a move. A session:

```
#Clear
#Gripcal
#Gripinfo
#Gripvel 30
#Gripcur 300
#Grippos 200
#Grippos 20
```

The [UART reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/uart/) has these and the driver commands a gripper needs; the driver's
whole command set is on the [STEPFOC site](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/reference/uart/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/python/ -->

# With Python

The `Spectral-BLDC` library wraps the driver's CAN protocol, gripper messages included: one method per message,
and the gripper's answers unpacked into attributes. The ROS 2 driver and the legacy gripper GUI are built on it.

## Installing

```
pip install Spectral-BLDC
```

The source and the examples are in [Spectral-BLDC-Python](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python).

## The first program

```python
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import time

# the adapter: a CANvas on COM20 (Windows) or /dev/ttyACM0 (Linux), 1 Mbit/s
bus = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM20', bitrate=1000000)
gripper = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=bus)

gripper.Send_Clear_Error()
gripper.Send_gripper_calibrate()
time.sleep(10)                                  # the jaws open fully, then close fully

for position in (200, 20, 200, 20):
    # position 0..255, speed 0..255, current mA, activate, action, E-stop, release direction
    gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(position, 30, 300, 1, 1, 0, 0)
    for _ in range(40):                         # poll the state for up to 2 s
        gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack()        # an empty frame: status only
        message, ids = bus.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.05)
        if message is not None:
            gripper.UnpackData(message, ids)
            print(gripper.gripper_position, gripper.gripper_current, gripper.gripper_object_detection)
            if gripper.gripper_object_detection in (1, 2, 3):   # object found, or at the position
                break
```

`Send_gripper_data_pack` with all seven arguments sends the move; without arguments it sends the empty status
poll. `receive_can_messages` returns the raw `python-can` message and the node ID, command ID and error bit from
the identifier; `UnpackData` fills the gripper attributes:

| Attribute | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `gripper_position` | 0 open to 255 closed |
| `gripper_current` | the motor current in mA |
| `gripper_activated`, `gripper_action_status` | the activate flag; 1 while a move is in progress |
| `gripper_object_detection` | 0 moving, 1 object found while closing, 2 object found while opening, 3 at the position |
| `gripper_temperature_error`, `gripper_timeout_error`, `gripper_estop_error` | the three error bits |
| `gripper_calibrated` | the gripper calibration is done |

!!! note "Object detection in library 1.20"
    Library version 1.20 assembles `gripper_object_detection` with its two bits swapped relative to the firmware:
    it reports 1 where the gripper sends 2 (object found while opening) and 2 where it sends 1 (object found
    while closing); 0 and 3 are unaffected. Until the library is fixed, swap the two values in your program, or
    test for "1 or 2" as this example does.

## Stopping

```python
gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(20, 30, 300, 1, 1, 1, 0)   # the E-stop bit: stops, raises the E-stop error
gripper.Send_Clear_Error()                                 # clears it; the next command must have the bit at 0
gripper.Send_Watchdog(500)                                 # from now on the gripper stops 500 ms after the last frame
```

With the watchdog set, keep the status poll running at a steady rate; a program that crashes releases the grip
within the watchdog time.

## Several grippers

One `CanCommunication` per bus, one `SpectralCAN` per gripper with its node ID; every answer carries the node ID
in `ids.node_id`, so route it to the right object. The [teleoperation guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/guides/teleoperation/) couples
two grippers this way.

The complete map of calls to messages is in the [Python library](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/python/) reference.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/ros2/ -->

# With ROS 2

The [msg_gripper_ros2](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/source_robotics_msg_gripper_ros2) package is a ROS 2
Humble driver for the gripper, built on the Python library and a `python-can` adapter. It was developed by the
UCLA Biomechatronics Lab and Ben Forbes, and is MIT licensed.

## What it offers

| Direction | Topic or action | Type |
|---|---|---|
| Command | `/gripper/command_joint_states` | `sensor_msgs/JointState`, the position as the gripper's own units, 0 to 255 |
| Feedback | `/gripper/feedback_joint_states` | `sensor_msgs/JointState`, the position in the same units and the effort in mA |
| Action | `/gripper_command` | `control_msgs/GripperCommand` |

## Installing

Ubuntu 22.04 with ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 or newer, and a USB-to-CAN adapter that speaks slcan, such as the
CANvas:

```bash
pip install Spectral_BLDC python-can
cd ~/ros2_ws/src
git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/source_robotics_msg_gripper_ros2.git
cd ~/ros2_ws
colcon build --packages-select msg_gripper_ros2
source install/setup.bash
```

On Linux, add yourself to the `dialout` group to open the adapter's port without `sudo`, and log in again.

## Running

```bash
ros2 launch msg_gripper_ros2 msg_gripper_launch.py
```

The only setting that depends on your machine is the adapter's port, `channel` in `config/default.yaml`:
`/dev/ttyACM0` or `/dev/ttyUSB0` on Linux, `/dev/tty.usbmodem*` on macOS, `COM3` on Windows. Copy the file,
change it, and pass it at launch:

```bash
ros2 launch msg_gripper_ros2 msg_gripper_launch.py config_file:=~/my_gripper.yaml node_name:=my_gripper namespace:=robot
```

The package's README has the rest: the parameters, the node names, and the platforms it was tested on.

## The SSG-48 package

The [ssg48_adaptive_electric_gripper_ros2](https://github.com/Lass6230/ssg48_adaptive_electric_gripper_ros2)
package, written for the SSG-48 gripper, speaks the same protocol and should work with the MSG as well.

## The description files

The URDF and the MJCF of the gripper for ROS 2, Gazebo and MuJoCo are in the product repository's
[MSG_gripper_description](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/MSG_gripper_description).

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/robots/ -->

# On PAROL6 and PAR6

The gripper is made for the Source Robotics arms. Both drive it over their own CAN bus; their software calibrates
it, moves it and reads its state, so a program for the robot does not talk CAN itself.

## PAROL6

1. Mount the gripper with the `ring_cover-PAROL6` part ([Mounting on a robot](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/04-installation/mounting/)).
2. Connect it with the [PAROL6 gripper cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/gripper-cable) to the
   robot's gripper port. Only this cable: the PAR6 cable is wired differently and destroys the gripper
   ([The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/04-installation/cable/)).
3. Keep the gripper's node ID at 0 and set its termination switch ON; it is the last node on the robot's bus.

The PAROL6 commander software has the electric gripper's controls: calibrate, then a position, a speed and a
current for a move, and the gripper's status. The PAROL6 Python API drives it as a tool, from a program:

```python
rbt.select_tool("MSG", variant_key="150mm")           # the parol6 package; 100mm, 150mm or 200mm, the rail
rbt.tool.calibrate()                                   # queued with the motion; lasts a few seconds
rbt.tool.set_position(0.8, speed=0.5, current=0.4)     # fractions of the ranges
print(rbt.tool.status())
```

The [PAROL6 documentation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/) covers the robot's side: the gripper
port, the commander software and the API.

## PAR6

The PAR6 arm's control box runs the gripper on its CAN bus as a tool, with the PAR6 gripper cable (different from
the PAROL6 one). The [PAR6 documentation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/par6/) covers the tool configuration,
the runtime's gripper commands and the firmware updates the box can do for the gripper.

## Another robot

Any controller with a CAN interface drives the gripper directly: [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/can/) is the protocol,
[With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/python/) and [With ROS 2](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/ros2/) are two ready implementations, and the
[CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/) has every byte.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/errors/ -->

# Errors and recovery

When the driver inside the gripper detects a fault it stops the motor, goes to idle and sets the error bit in
every CAN frame it sends. The grip is released: an idle stepper holds nothing beyond the mechanism's friction.

## Seeing the error

- **The error bit** of every answer's identifier: 1 while any error is active.
- **Respond_Gripper_data_pack** carries the three gripper error bits: temperature, timeout, E-stop.
- **Send_Respond_State_of_Errors** returns every flag of the driver, which is where the other causes show.
- Motor GUI shows the errors in its gripper panel; `#Error` over UART prints them.

## The errors

| Error | Reported in | Cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Temperature | the gripper's temperature bit | the thermistor on the motor housing reads more than 75 °C (`#Tlim`) | let the motor cool; hold with less current |
| Timeout | the gripper's timeout bit | the driver's CAN watchdog ran out: no valid frame within the time set by Send_Watchdog | the host stopped sending; fix the host, then clear |
| E-stop | the gripper's E-stop bit | a move command with the E-stop bit set, or `#Gripstop 1` | clear, then send a command with the bit at 0: a command with the bit still set raises it again |
| Not calibrated (motor) | State_of_Errors, `#Error` | the driver's own motor calibration is missing: a self-built gripper before [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/first-run/), or after `#Default` | calibrate the motor |
| Vbus | State_of_Errors | the supply is below 9 V or above 29.5 V | the supply, the cable |
| Encoder | State_of_Errors | the driver's encoder does not see its magnet | the magnet on the stepper shaft (a self-built gripper) |
| Driver | State_of_Errors | the driver stage's own protection tripped: overcurrent, overtemperature | lower the current; check the motor leads |
| Velocity | State_of_Errors | the motor exceeded the driver's speed limit | unlikely in a gripper; clear |
| Driver E-stop | State_of_Errors | Send_ESTOP was received | clear |

A gripper that is not **gripper-calibrated** is not in error: it just refuses moves until Send_gripper_calibrate
has found the end stops.

## Clearing

Send_Clear_Error, **Clear** in the GUI or `#Clear` clears every flag, the gripper's E-stop included, and goes to
idle. An error whose cause is still present comes straight back: a hot motor, a supply that is still low. After
an E-stop, the next move command must carry the E-stop bit at 0, or the error is raised again at once.

After clearing, the gripper is idle and still calibrated and activated; the next move command moves it.

## When the gripper does not answer

- No answer at all: the supply, the cable (and its pinout), the bus termination (about 60 Ω across CANH and CANL
  with everything unpowered), 1 Mbit/s on the adapter, the node ID.
- Answers but does not move: not calibrated, not activated, an error active, or the action bit at 0.
- Moves to one end during calibration and stops there: the other end stop is blocked, or the mechanism is too
  stiff for the calibration's 500 mA; after 24 seconds the routine gives up.

[Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/09-troubleshooting/) goes through the symptoms one by one.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/07-maintenance/ -->

# Maintenance

The gripper needs little: every wearing part is printed, so a worn part is replaced by printing a new one, and
the mechanism is a rail, two racks and a pinion that want a little grease now and then. Power the gripper off
before any work on it.

## Before each session

- The jaws sit tight on their carriers, nothing is cracked, the pads or the sponge tape are whole.
- The cable's M8 nut is tight, the cable has slack for the wrist's full motion and runs clear of the jaws.
- Nothing lies in the jaws' travel, and the gripper calibration finds both end stops.

## When the motion gets rough, and every few months of regular use

- **Grease.** A little lithium grease on the rail and on the rack and pinion. Remove the four screws that hold
  the linear rail to reach the mechanism, wipe off the old grease and the dust, grease, refit, and move the jaws
  over the whole stroke by hand before you power up. A grinding noise, a stiff motion or a calibration that
  stops short of an end are the signs that it is due.
- **Clean** with a dry cloth. The gripper is not waterproof or dustproof: keep it out of wet and dusty places,
  and blow chips out of the rail rather than wash them out.
- **Screws**: the jaw screws, the rail screws and the clamp screws of the shaft coupler; threadlocker where the
  assembly instructions use it.
- **The camera lens**, with a lens cloth.

## Replacing worn parts

The jaws, the pads and every other printed part are in the product repository,
[Print files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/Print%20files); the
rail, the carriages, the pinion and the screws are in the
[BOM](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/blob/main/BOM.md). A replacement jaw
is the same part as a new one, and the gripper calibration at the next power-up takes care of the end stops.

A stepper or a driver is not serviced but replaced: the stepper by one of the three in the BOM, after which the
motor calibration of [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/first-run/) is run again; the driver by a new
[STEPFOC driver](https://source-robotics.com/products/stepfoc-stepper-controller), configured the same way.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/08-firmware/ -->

# Firmware

The gripper has no firmware of its own: it runs the STEPFOC driver's firmware with gripper mode turned on. This
site describes the firmware release named in the version box on the landing page, for the gripper release the
site is versioned by; a new firmware release for the same gripper updates these pages in place.

## Which release does my gripper run?

Over CAN, Send_Respond_Device_Info returns the firmware version as its third byte; over UART, `#Info` prints
`Software version: <number>`. The [compatibility table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/appendix/compatibility/) says which releases go with
which Python library and bootloader.

## Updating

A gripper shipped with firmware 104 or newer carries the driver's bootloader and updates over its CAN cable: the
host tells the driver to reset, the bootloader waits two seconds for a host, and the host streams the new image
into it. Nothing is opened. The image is `stepfoc-firmware-V<number>.bin` from the driver's
[GitHub releases](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/STEPFOC-stepper-controller/releases), with a manifest
`firmware.json` and the release notes.

| From | How |
|---|---|
| a PC with the CANvas adapter | [Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/) over CAN: choose the release, the GUI fetches the image and flashes it |
| a PC, scripted | `host_tools/bl_flash.py` from the [bootloader repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/stm32f103c-bootloader), over CAN (slcan or gs_usb adapters) or over the driver's UART port |
| a PAR6 control box | the box updates every device on its bus, the gripper included, from its dashboard or `tools/flash_motor_firmware.py` |

The procedure, the bootloader's protocol and what to do when a flash is interrupted are in the STEPFOC
documentation: [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/07-firmware/update/)
and [The bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/07-firmware/the-bootloader/).

!!! warning "Before you update"
    - Open the gripper or take the object out: it loses its grip during the update and until it is calibrated
      and commanded again.
    - An update may clear the driver's configuration (the release notes say so when it does). A bought gripper's
      configuration is in [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/first-run/), so it can be restored; note
      what `#Info` prints before you start.
    - Give the gripper a node ID from 0 to 13: the bootloader cannot address 14 or 15.

A gripper whose driver runs firmware 103 or older has no bootloader; it is updated once with a programming
adapter on the driver's JTAG pads, inside the housing, as described in
[Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/07-firmware/bootloader/).
From then on it updates over CAN like any other.

## Release notes

The release notes of every STEPFOC release up to the one this site describes are in the appendix,
[Firmware release notes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/appendix/firmware-release-notes/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/09-troubleshooting/ -->

# Troubleshooting

By symptom. The error flags and what clears them are in [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/errors/).

## The gripper does not answer

| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| nothing at all | the 24 V on the cable; the cable's pinout (a wrong one has destroyed the driver already); the node ID the host uses; 1 Mbit/s on the adapter; the termination (about 60 Ω across CANH and CANL, unpowered) |
| answers, then stops answering | the watchdog ran out and the host did not notice; a loose M8 connector; a second device with the same node ID |
| the GUI shows *No connection* | the COM port of the CANvas adapter; another program holding the port; the CAN ID in the GUI |

## It does not move

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A([The gripper does not move]) --> B{Does it answer on CAN?}
    B -- no --> C[24 V on the cable, the pinout, the node ID,<br>1 Mbit/s, the termination]
    B -- yes --> D{Calibrated?}
    D -- no --> E[Run the gripper calibration;<br>a self-built gripper: the stepper calibration first]
    D -- yes --> F{An error flag set?}
    F -- yes --> G[Clear it; if it comes back,<br>Errors and recovery names the cause]
    F -- no --> H{Activate and action bits at 1?}
    H -- no --> I[Send the command with activate = 1 and action = 1]
    H -- yes --> J[The command equals the previous one:<br>change the speed or the current by one]
```

| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| calibrated, activated, no error, no motion | the action bit of the command is 0; the command is identical to the previous one (change the speed or the current by one to repeat a move) |
| *Not calibrated* after power-up | normal: run the gripper calibration |
| an error is shown | [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/errors/): clear it, then look at the cause if it comes back |
| the driver reports *Not calibrated* in State_of_Errors and `#Error` | the stepper itself is not calibrated (a self-built gripper): [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/first-run/) |

## Calibration

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| the jaws move to one end and stop; after 24 s the gripper is still not calibrated | the other end is blocked, or the mechanism is too stiff for the calibration's 500 mA: a tight rail, a pinion pressed too hard into the racks, debris in the racks |
| the jaws jitter and do not travel | a phase of the stepper not connected (self-built), or the stepper not calibrated |
| 255 is not fully closed, or 0 not fully open | something stopped the jaws short of the end during calibration; calibrate again with the stroke free |

## The grip

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| the object slips | the current too low for the object; the jaw faces: sponge tape or the TPU pad |
| the object is crushed | the current too high; a hard object takes the full force at once |
| *object detected* while nothing is there | the current limit too low for the mechanism's friction at that speed; raise the current a little or lower the speed |
| the gripper stops with a temperature error after a while | a long hold at a high current; hold with the lowest current that keeps the object |
| the jaws creep or hum when holding | the position loop against a hard object; lower the current, or hold a soft object with a position slightly beyond the contact |

## Noise and heat

A stepper under field-oriented control is quiet; a grinding noise is the rack and pinion without grease, or
debris. The motor gets warm in use and hot under a long grip; the thermistor stops it at 75 °C. A self-built
gripper without the thermistor on its motor has no such protection.

## After a firmware update

If the gripper does not calibrate or behaves oddly after an update, check the driver's configuration with
`#Info` over UART: gripper mode (`#Gripper 1`), the thermistor (`#Term 1`), the motor calibration. A release note
says when an update clears the configuration; [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/first-run/) restores
it.

## Getting help

[Support](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/support/) says where to ask and what to include; the gripper's status and `#Info`'s output are
the first things.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/ -->

# Build guide

**The MSG is open source, and that is important to us.** Everything the gripper is made of is published in the
[product repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper) under the CERN Open
Hardware Licence: the STEP and print files of every part, the bill of materials with a link for every item, the
assembly video, and the URDF and MJCF models. The driver's firmware and the software that drives the gripper are
open source too. A gripper you build is the same gripper as the one from the shop, and this manual applies to
it; change the jaws, the camera mount or the body for your application, or fit the gripper to a robot it was not
designed for. This guide is the order to do it in.

!!! warning
    A self-built gripper is yours to make safe: the thermistor on the motor, the current within the stepper's
    maximum, and the [Safety](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/02-safety/) chapter apply to it as to a bought one. The gripper is in beta:
    expect rough edges in the hardware and the software.

## The steps

1. Choose a rail length for the stroke and a stepper length for the force: [Variants](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/01-overview/variants/).
2. [Bill of materials](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/bill-of-materials/): the repository's BOM, with the reference images.
3. [Printing the parts](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/printing/): PETG at 25 % infill, the folders for your rail and stepper, the jaws.
4. [Mechanical assembly](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/mechanical-assembly/): the video, the order, the cable.
5. [Driver setup and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/first-run/): the motor calibration before the pinion goes in, gripper mode,
   the thermistor, the first moves.

## Kits and the shop

You do not have to source everything yourself:

| | What is in it | You add |
|---|---|---|
| [STEPFOC starter kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/stepfoc-starter-kit) | the STEPFOC driver, the CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter, the USB-to-serial adapter, an ST-Link with the programming adapter, the UART, power and CAN cables, the 6 × 2.5 mm encoder magnet, the 100K thermistor | the stepper, the rail and its carriages, the pinion, the shaft coupler, the M8 connector, the screws and inserts, the camera, the printed parts |
| [STEPFOC driver](https://source-robotics.com/products/stepfoc-stepper-controller) alone | the driver | the rest, and the adapters its setup needs |
| [Assembled MSG gripper](https://source-robotics.com/products/msg-gripper) | the gripper, built, calibrated and configured, in the rail, stepper and colour you choose | the [cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/gripper-cable) |

The starter kit is the good-value start for a build: it has the driver and everything the driver's setup needs,
the CAN adapter for Motor GUI, the serial adapter for the UART, the magnet, the thermistor and the two internal
cables, for little more than the driver alone. The [PAROL6 gripper cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/gripper-cable)
is in the shop too.

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/printing/ -->

# Printing the parts

## Material and settings

PETG for every part but the TPU jaw pads. The repository's print table is one line, and it is the whole rule:
**use 25 % infill for all** ([Print_table.md](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/blob/main/Print_table.md)).
Supports where your slicer asks for them; the body prints on its back.

## The files

| Variant | Folders in [STEP files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files) |
|---|---|
| every gripper | [`Common parts`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files/Common%20parts): the coupler plate and ring cover (or `ring_cover-PAROL6`), the camera mount and lid, the jaw blocker, the stepper spacer, the connector lid |
| your rail | [`Linear rail dependant parts`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files/Linear%20rail%20dependant%20parts)`/<rail>`: the body and the two jaw carriers |
| your stepper | [`Stepper dependant parts`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files/Stepper%20dependant%20parts)`/<stepper>`: the stepper cover, and the spacer for the 21.5 mm stepper |
| the jaws | [`Gripper jaws attachment`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files/Gripper%20jaws%20attachment): one of the designs, mirrored for the other side |

The [Print files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/Print%20files)
folder has the same parts as 3MF, ready to slice.

## The jaws

Two kinds, both in `Gripper jaws attachment`; mirror the file in the slicer for the other side:

- **TPU jaws** (recommended): a PETG body, `MSG_JAW_TPU_GLUE`, and a soft TPU pad printed separately and glued
  on. The pad deforms around the object for a gentler, surer grip. Print the pad with **16 % infill, no top or
  bottom layers and 2 walls** for the softest grip; the body with the normal settings.
- **Solid jaws**: `MSG_SOLID_JAW` in one piece, or `MSG_JAW_HOLLOW` for a two-colour print; `MSG_JAW_TPU_GLUE`
  prints solid too.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The TPU jaw in the slicer](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/assets/jaw_slicer1.webp){ width="520" }
  ![The TPU pad's settings](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/assets/jaw_slicer2.webp){ width="520" }
  <figcaption>Figure 16: The TPU jaw: the PETG body and the TPU pad as separate prints, and the pad's settings.</figcaption>
</figure>

Gluing the pad on, its orientation and the sponge tape for the gripping faces are in
[Jaws](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/04-installation/jaws/); the repository's
[jaw guide](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/blob/main/Assembly%20manual/Building_gripper_jaws.md)
is the original.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/mechanical-assembly/ -->

# Mechanical assembly

The assembly is shown in the repository's video; a PDF manual is in preparation. Watch the video once before you
start, with the parts in front of you.

<iframe width="100%" height="460" src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/oAUhDKYgLso" title="MSG gripper assembly" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture" allowfullscreen></iframe>

[Open the video on YouTube](https://youtu.be/oAUhDKYgLso)

## The order

1. The driver first: calibrated, in gripper mode, with the thermistor, as [Driver setup and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/first-run/)
   describes. The motor calibration turns the stepper several revolutions, which the racks cannot follow, so it
   happens before the pinion meshes.
2. The brass inserts into the printed parts with a soldering iron.
3. The rail with its two carriages into the body, the racks onto the carriers.
4. The stepper, with the pinion on its shaft and the driver on its back, into the body so that the pinion meshes
   with both racks; the thermistor's leads to the driver.
5. The driver's power and CAN cables to the M8 connector in its lid; the lid onto the body.
6. The stepper cover over the driver, with the termination switch reachable through its opening.
7. The coupler plate with the shaft coupler on the back, or `ring_cover-PAROL6` for the PAROL6 wrist.
8. The jaws onto the carriers, the camera into its mount.

## The cable

The gripper's cable is not in the box. [The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/04-installation/cable/) has the parts, the wiring
diagrams for PAROL6 and PAR6, and the warning that the two are not interchangeable; the repository's
[cable guide](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/blob/main/Assembly%20manual/Building_cables.md)
is the original.

## The jaws

Printing, gluing and padding the jaws: [Printing the parts](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/printing/) and [Jaws](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/04-installation/jaws/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/build/first-run/ -->

# Driver setup and first run

A gripper from the shop arrives with its driver configured: the stepper calibrated, gripper mode on, the
thermistor on, the gains set, everything saved. A gripper you build has a bare STEPFOC driver that must be
brought to the same state once, over its UART port. This page is that procedure; the commands are the driver's,
and the [STEPFOC documentation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/) explains each in depth.

## What you need

- The driver mounted on the stepper with its encoder magnet, before the pinion is engaged in the racks: the
  motor calibration turns the motor several revolutions in both directions, which the racks cannot follow. Do
  this step with the stepper out of the gripper or with the pinion not yet fitted.
- A 3.3 V [USB-to-serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter) on the driver's
  UART connector, a terminal at 256000 baud with CR+LF line endings, and 24 V on the driver's power connector.
  [The serial terminal](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/05-setup/terminal/) on the STEPFOC
  site shows the terminal setup.
- The thermistor from the BOM, soldered to the driver's thermistor connector and fixed to the motor housing
  with thermal cement.

## With Motor GUI

[Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/05-setup/motor-gui/), connected over **UART** through the serial adapter, has a preset per stepper on its
setup page: *MSG 21.5 mm motor*, *MSG 40 mm motor* and *MSG 60 mm motor*. A preset writes the stepper's
resistance, inductance and 50 pole pairs, the current limit, the loop gains, gripper mode, the thermistor and
the CAN ID, then saves; its CAN ID is 6, the PAR6 gripper's, so change it before applying for another robot.
Apply it after the motor calibration of step 1: it does step 2 for you.

## 1. The motor calibration

Restore the defaults first, so that nothing from another motor or junk in the EEPROM goes into the calibration,
then enter the stepper's parameters and calibrate:

| Stepper | `#PP` | `#R` | `#L` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21.5 mm, 17HS08-1004S | 50 | 3.7 | 0.0045 |
| 40 mm, 17HS16-2004S1 | 50 | 1.1 | 0.0026 |
| 60 mm, 17HS24-2104S | 50 | 1.6 | 0.0030 |

```
#Default
#PP 50
#R 1.1
#L 0.0026
#Cal
```

The motor turns, the driver prints each step and ends with `Calibration success!`. The whole routine and its
messages are in [Calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/05-setup/calibration/) on
the STEPFOC site. `#Default` also resets the serial number the driver reports; note what `#Info` printed if you
need it.

## 2. The gripper settings

```
#Gripper 1
#Term 1
#Tlim 75
#Kpiq 1.4047
#Kiiq 0.1149
#CANID 0
#Save
```

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `#Gripper 1` | gripper mode: the driver runs the gripper state machine and answers the gripper messages |
| `#Term 1`, `#Tlim 75` | the thermistor on, the temperature limit at 75 °C. Without it the motor can burn out under a long grip |
| `#Kpiq 1.4047`, `#Kiiq 0.1149` | the current loop gains of Motor GUI's gripper presets, the same for the three steppers; the gains the calibration computes for the stepper are sharper than a gripper needs |
| `#CANID 0` | the node ID on the robot's bus; 0 to 13, see [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/can/) |
| `#Save` | nothing above survives a power cycle until it is saved |

## 3. Assemble and calibrate the gripper

Fit the pinion and assemble the gripper, power it up, and run the gripper calibration (`#Gripcal`, or Motor GUI's
**Calibrate**): the jaws open fully and close fully. Then a first move at a low current, as in
[Calibrate, activate, move](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/05-setup/first-moves/). `#Gripinfo` prints the gripper's state, including the end stops the
calibration found.

## Current limit

The gripper's moves use the current limit of each command, not the driver's `#Ilim`. Keep the commanded current
at or below the stepper's maximum current ([Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/)); the
firmware does not clamp it.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/appendix/performance/ -->

# Performance tests

Thermal tests of the MSG gripper under different conditions. The thermal limit is 75 °C at the thermistor on the
motor housing.

!!! warning
    A gripper built without the thermistor on its motor has no temperature protection and can damage its motor
    in normal operation.

## Several days of cycling

- Open and close every 2.5 s, no load: the current near 0
- 7 days without interruption
- Motor temperature: 42 °C
- Ambient temperature: 33 °C

## Holding at a constant current

- Hold an object at a constant current for 24 hours
- Current setpoint: to be published
- Stable motor temperature: to be published
- Ambient temperature: to be published

## The current that trips the thermal limit

- Hold an object at a high current until the temperature error trips
- Current setpoint and the time to the error: to be published
- Ambient temperature: to be published

The results of the two open tests, and the measured force-against-current curves for the three steppers, will be
added here as they are made.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/appendix/firmware-release-notes/ -->

# Firmware release notes

What changed in each release of the STEPFOC firmware the gripper runs, from the release notes in the driver's
repository, up to the release this site describes. Entries about the driver's motion modes do not concern a
gripper; the gripper mode, the CAN protocol and the bootloader do.

## V108 (2026-08-26)

STEPFOC firmware **V108** — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader.

#### Bug fixes
- Fixed calibration (`#Cal`) spuriously failing with `Phase order is wrong!` on otherwise-healthy motors. The "confirm commutation" pre-check (before the real angle-offset search) commands a pure torque-axis voltage using the not-yet-calibrated encoder angle — depending on a given unit's actual rotor-to-encoder mounting angle, that command could land almost entirely on the wrong axis and produce ~zero torque, failing the check even though nothing was actually broken. Bench-confirmed on a real unit.
- Fix: retry the pre-check once at a 90° angle bias before declaring failure — guaranteed to land within 45° of the true torque axis on at least one of the two tries. The downstream angle-offset search is unaffected and already independent of this pre-check.
- Added `Spin-confirm delta` / `Vbus` diagnostics to `#Cal`'s failure report, for the rare case both tries still fail.

#### Assets
- `stepfoc-firmware-V108.bin` — application firmware image (flash at `0x08003000`, target STM32F103CB).
- `firmware.json` — manifest with version, size, and SHA-256 for download verification by the web flasher.

#### Integrity
- SHA-256: `25cbc4887ca2c192eba6e708930eb6b6c677fd1e76299313c3b3ce3459e0e8a1`
- Size: 99188 bytes

Built from commit 46b4911 on `bootloader-version`. Includes bootloader entry support (CAN/UART reset-into-bootloader).

## V107 (2026-08-24)

STEPFOC firmware **V107** — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader.

#### Bug fixes
- Fixed PD mode (`IN_DATA_PACK_PD` over CAN): the commanded speed was written into `Feedforward_speed`, but `PD_mode()` reads `Velocity_setpoint` for its KD term — so the KD (velocity-damping) term of the impedance controller was always evaluated against a stale/zero setpoint and had no effect. The CAN handler now writes the field the control law actually reads. `IN_DATA_PACK_1` / position mode is unaffected — `Feedforward_speed` there is correct and continues to feed the position cascade.

#### CAN bus
- Added a generic settings command (`IN_SETTINGS`) so future boolean settings don't each need their own command ID. Payload is `mask` + `value` (one byte each), one bit per setting — only bits set in the mask are applied, so a sender only needs to know about the bits it cares about.
- First setting on this command: brake vs. coast (bit 0), previously only selectable over UART (`Brake` / `Coast`), now selectable over CAN as well.

#### Assets
- `stepfoc-firmware-V107.bin` — application firmware image (flash at `0x08003000`, target STM32F103CB).
- `firmware.json` — manifest with version, size, and SHA-256 for download verification by the web flasher.

#### Integrity
- SHA-256: `63699037c79318e1d78738edcb13e9f9bc00a3393dc5803f920b244a60622ae2`
- Size: 98972 bytes

Built from commit 04ec180 on `bootloader-version`. Includes bootloader entry support (CAN/UART reset-into-bootloader).

## V106 (2026-07-05)

STEPFOC firmware **V106** — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader.

#### CAN bus
- The controller now drains up to 8 CAN messages per pass instead of just 1, so short bursts (multiple commands sent back-to-back, or a busy multi-node bus) no longer silently drop messages once the 3-deep hardware FIFO fills.
- A CAN peripheral that fails to initialize no longer bricks the board — UART stays fully usable, only the CAN bus is skipped.

#### Safety
- Added a hardware watchdog (100ms). If the control loop ever stops running, the board resets instead of leaving the motor driven at a stale duty cycle.
- Fixed a bug where `Torque_mode` could silently overwrite your commanded Iq setpoint when clamping to the current limit — reading it back after clamping now shows what you actually asked for, and raising the current limit afterward immediately restores the original commanded torque instead of requiring the command to be resent.
- Fixed undefined behavior in a serial-protocol integer conversion (`fourBytesToInt`).
- Synced default configuration values that had drifted between two locations in the code, so a fresh `#Default` and a freshly-flashed board's built-in defaults now agree.

#### EEPROM / configuration integrity
- Added CRC validation over the saved configuration, split into two independent halves: **calibration data** (resistance, inductance, Kt/KV, angle offset, current-loop gains, etc.) and **settings** (PID tuning, limits, watchdog config, CAN ID, etc.).
- This means a corrupted save (e.g. from a power loss mid-write) is detected and safely defaulted instead of silently running with garbage values — and critically, a *future* firmware update that only adds a new setting can no longer wipe your calibration, since the two are validated independently.
- Boards upgrading from older, pre-CRC firmware keep their existing calibration automatically — no need to recalibrate after this update.
- A few unused slots were reserved in the calibration block for upcoming features (e.g. magnet alignment), so those can be added later without another migration.

#### Performance
- PWM output no longer re-resolves which timer/channel it's writing to on every single call (it was doing this 4x per control tick) — resolved once and cached, freeing up ISR headroom.
- Velocity calculation switched from a floating-point divide to an integer multiply.

#### Usability
- New `#Help` command — prints a summary of the available commands.
- Serial now responds with "Unknown command" for unrecognized input instead of silently ignoring it.
- Calibration now prints progress during the angle-offset search (previously up to ~40 seconds of silence that could look like the board had hung).
- `#Error` now also reports driver faults (undervoltage/thermal/overcurrent), not just the other error types.
- `#Info` now always reports live ISR execution time, useful for checking control-loop headroom on the bench.

#### Assets
- `stepfoc-firmware-V106.bin` — application firmware image (flash at `0x08003000`, target STM32F103CB).
- `firmware.json` — manifest with version, size, and SHA-256 for download verification by the web flasher.

#### Integrity
- SHA-256: `bc061fb273e7c836e3180fa597ecd373e7e357b0eab9130b63a7fd19b70a6073`
- Size: 98940 bytes

Built from commit 661e7d3 on `bootloader-version`. Includes bootloader entry support (CAN/UART reset-into-bootloader).

## V105 (2026-07-04)

STEPFOC firmware **V105** — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader.

#### What's new
- Reversed stepper phase wiring now calibrates automatically — no more "switch phases and try again." The firmware detects the wiring and compensates it in software, so **all 8 phase-wiring permutations calibrate identically and symmetrically**.
- `#Info` now reports the firmware's own build version, so the version is correct immediately after flashing (no `#Default` needed).

#### Assets
- `stepfoc-firmware-V105.bin` — application firmware image (flash at `0x08003000`, target STM32F103CB).
- `firmware.json` — manifest with version, size, and SHA-256 for download verification by the web flasher.

#### Integrity
- SHA-256: `0d80ce3cf78109f6ff54697425ed475ffca4e97e220d72fe0823ce1bd60a4908`
- Size: 95924 bytes

Built from commit bda57d6 on `bootloader-version`. Includes bootloader entry support (CAN/UART reset-into-bootloader).

## V103 (2025-12-28)

First stable release for public

## V102 (2025-12-28)

First official release for the public

## V101 (2025-09-29)

Initial fully functional release based on spectral micro firmware.

# Versions and compatibility

Which STEPFOC firmware release works with which bootloader, gripper hardware, Python library and ROS 2 driver.
One row per firmware release, newest first; the last column names the version of this site, a gripper release, that
describes it.

| Firmware (STEPFOC) | Released | Bootloader | MSG gripper | Python library (Spectral-BLDC) | ROS 2 driver | Docs (gripper release) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 108 | 2026-08-26 | required (installed on grippers shipped with 104 or newer) | V1.1 | 1.20 or newer | msg_gripper_ros2 (ROS 2 Humble) | 1.1 |
| 107 | 2026-08-24 | required | V1.1 | 1.20 or newer | msg_gripper_ros2 | not published |

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/terminology/ -->

# Glossary

**Action bit**
:   A bit of the move command: 1 carries out the move, 0 leaves the gripper idle with the command stored.

**Activated**
:   A flag the gripper keeps, set by the activate bit of the move command or by `#Gripact`. A move is carried out
    only while the gripper is activated and calibrated.

**CAN ID** (node ID)
:   The address of the gripper on the CAN bus, 0 to 13; every gripper ships as 0. It occupies bits 10 to 7 of the
    11-bit CAN frame identifier; the command ID occupies bits 6 to 1 and the error bit is bit 0.

**CANvas**
:   Source Robotics' USB-to-CAN adapter. It appears as a serial port and speaks slcan, which `python-can`, Motor
    GUI and the ROS 2 driver use.

**Current limit** (grip force)
:   The current, in mA, the driver may put into the motor during a move. Torque is current times the motor's
    torque constant, so the current limit sets the force with which the jaws press on an object.

**Driver**
:   The STEPFOC board on the back of the gripper's stepper: field-oriented control of the motor, the gripper state
    machine and the CAN and UART interfaces. The gripper's firmware is the driver's firmware.

**E-stop bit**
:   A bit of the move command. 1 stops the gripper and raises the gripper E-stop error, which stays until it is
    cleared and a command with the bit at 0 arrives.

**Error bit**
:   Bit 0 of every CAN frame identifier the driver sends: 1 while any error is active.

**Field-oriented control** (FOC)
:   Controlling the stepper's current as a vector relative to the rotor, from the driver's encoder. It turns the
    stepper into a motor whose torque is known and limited, which is what makes a force-controlled gripper out
    of it.

**Firmware release**
:   One build of the STEPFOC firmware, numbered 103, 104, 105, … and tagged `V103`, `V104`, … in the driver's
    repository. `#Info` prints the release a gripper runs. This documentation describes one release; the version
    selector switches between them.

**Gripper calibration**
:   The routine (`Send_gripper_calibrate`, `#Gripcal`) that opens the jaws fully, then closes them fully, at low
    force, and records both end stops as positions 0 and 255. Needed after every power-up.

**Gripper mode**
:   The driver's mode in which it runs a gripper (`#Gripper 1`, saved): move commands with a jaw position, a speed
    and a current limit, and object detection.

**Motor calibration**
:   The driver's own calibration of the stepper (`#Cal`): the pole pairs, resistance and inductance entered, the
    encoder aligned, the motor constants measured. Done once, at the factory or when you build the gripper; not
    to be confused with the gripper calibration.

**Object detection**
:   The gripper's report of why the jaws stopped: 0 still moving, 1 an object stopped them while closing, 2 an
    object stopped them while opening, 3 they reached the commanded position.

**Position**
:   The jaw position as the gripper commands and reports it: 0 fully open, 255 fully closed, linear in between.

**Rack and pinion**
:   The gripper's mechanism: a pinion on the motor shaft meshes with two racks that run on the linear rail in
    opposite directions, so one motor moves both jaws symmetrically.

**Speed**
:   The speed of a move, 0 to 255, mapped by the firmware to 500 to 60000 encoder ticks per second of the motor.

**Stroke**
:   How far each jaw carrier travels from fully open to fully closed: 55, 105 or 155 mm, set by the rail length.

**Timeout error** (watchdog)
:   The driver's CAN watchdog, as the gripper reports it: when the watchdog is set (`Send_Watchdog`) and no valid
    frame arrives in time, the gripper stops and raises it.

**Watchdog**
:   A timer the driver resets with every valid CAN frame it receives. When it is set and runs out, the gripper
    reports a timeout error and stops.

# API reference

The gripper's CAN messages and UART commands, its status and error bits, and the Python library calls that send
them, for the firmware named on the landing page. The gripper is a STEPFOC stepper driver in gripper mode and accepts the
driver's whole command set; only what a gripper host or a self-built gripper needs is here, the rest is in the
[STEPFOC reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/reference/).

- [CAN messages](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/): the identifier, and the gripper, system and status messages
- [UART commands](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/uart/): the gripper commands, the driver setup commands, status and utility
- [Errors and status bits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/errors/)
- [Python library](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/python/): which library call sends which message

**Conventions.** Bytes are numbered from 0 and multi-byte values are big-endian. Bits are numbered from the most
significant: bit 7 is the first flag in a byte. The position is 0 (open) to 255 (closed), the speed 0 to 255, the
current in mA. UART command names are case-sensitive.

The command IDs, frame lengths and responses are read from the firmware's source at its release tag when the site
is built, so they cannot drift from the firmware; the descriptions and byte layouts are written by hand.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can-tools/ -->

# CAN frame tool and downloads

Build or inspect a frame using the command definitions of this manual's firmware release. All calculations
run in your browser; the tool does not connect to an adapter or send commands to hardware.

## Downloads

[Command definitions (JSON)](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/assets/can/protocol-V108.json) · [Gripper DBC](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/assets/can/protocol-V108-gripper.dbc)

The JSON includes the firmware tag, source commit, message IDs, every documented layout and its bit order.
The DBC files cover **nodes 0 to 13**, with both the clean and fault-bit identifiers of driver replies.
Reserved commands are omitted. Values use the firmware's native units: ticks, ticks/s, mA and the units in
the [CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/).

An RTR request uses the same identifier as its data reply. DBC describes the **data reply**; it does not
represent the request's RTR flag or the empty gripper status poll. Both are supported by the browser tool.

The gripper's two object-detection bits have an unusual order: bit 5 is the low bit, bit 4 the high bit.
The DBC signal `gripper_object_detection_raw` retains the wire value and supplies text labels (raw 2 =
object while closing, raw 1 = object while opening). The browser decoder converts that pair to the firmware's
numeric status (1 = closing, 2 = opening).

## Try a frame

The example `0x07A`, data `C8 1E 01 2C C0`, is a command to gripper node 0: position 200, speed 30,
current 300 mA, activate and action set, E-stop and release direction clear. These are an illustration of the
encoding; the device's current and motion limits still apply. Select another message above the fields to build
one of its documented forms. To inspect a reply, enter its identifier and data bytes below.

<div class="can-tool" data-schema="../../assets/can/protocol-V108.json" markdown="0">
  <p class="can-tool__status" role="status">Loading the firmware's command definitions…</p>
  <fieldset><legend>Build a frame</legend>
    <label for="ct-node">Node ID (0–13)</label><input id="ct-node" name="node" type="number" min="0" max="13" step="1" value="0">
    <label for="ct-command">Message and layout</label><select id="ct-command" name="command"></select>
    <label><input name="error" type="checkbox"> Driver reply has an active fault (error bit 1)</label>
    <div class="can-tool__fields"></div>
    <button type="button" name="build" class="md-button md-button--primary">Build frame</button>
    <pre class="can-tool__built" aria-live="polite"></pre>
    <button type="button" name="use" class="md-button">Use this frame in the decoder</button>
  </fieldset>
  <fieldset><legend>Decode a frame</legend>
    <label for="ct-id">CAN identifier (hex)</label><input id="ct-id" name="identifier" type="text" value="0x07A" spellcheck="false">
    <label for="ct-data">Data bytes (hex, up to eight)</label><input id="ct-data" name="data" type="text" value="C8 1E 01 2C C0" spellcheck="false">
    <label><input name="remote" type="checkbox"> Remote request (RTR; no payload)</label>
    <button type="button" name="decode" class="md-button md-button--primary">Decode frame</button>
    <div class="can-tool__decoded" aria-live="polite"></div>
  </fieldset>
  <noscript>Enable JavaScript for the frame tool, or use the reference tables and downloads above.</noscript>
</div>

**Check:** the example decodes to the values above. Change the identifier to `0x1FA` to see the same command
addressed to node 3. An invalid length or out-of-range field produces an explanation instead of a frame.

For wiring, termination, host timing and recovery, use [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/can/). To look up a
message's purpose and accepted lengths, use the [CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/ -->

# CAN messages

CAN 2.0, 1 Mbit/s, 11-bit identifiers. The identifier carries the node ID (bits 10 to 7, 0 to 13), the command ID
(bits 6 to 1, 0 to 63) and, in frames from the gripper, the error bit (bit 0). [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/06-operation/can/)
explains how the pieces are used; this page lists them.

Three kinds of message:

- **Send_…** — the host sends data to the gripper. The gripper command is answered with Respond_Gripper_data_pack;
  the others are not answered.
- **Send_Respond_…** — the host asks for data with a **remote frame** (RTR bit set, no data) under the command ID;
  the gripper answers with a data frame under the same command ID.
- **Respond_…** — frames only the gripper sends.

Multi-byte values are big-endian (data[0] first); bits inside a byte are numbered from the most significant bit
(bit 7 first).

## The messages a gripper needs

| ID | Message | Direction | Length | Group |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | [Send_ESTOP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_estop) | host → driver | 0 | System |
| 1 | [Send_Clear_Error](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_clear_error) | host → driver | 0 | System |
| 9 | [Respond_Heartbeat](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/status/#respond_heartbeat) | driver → host | 0 | Status requests |
| 10 | [Send_Respond_Ping](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/status/#send_respond_ping) | host → driver as a remote frame, driver → host as a data frame | 0 (remote) / 0 | Status requests |
| 11 | [Send_CAN_ID](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_can_id) | host → driver | 1 | System |
| 12 | [Send_Idle](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_idle) | host → driver | 0 | System |
| 13 | [Send_Save_config](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_save_config) | host → driver | 0 | System |
| 14 | [Send_Reset](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_reset) | host → driver | 0 | System |
| 15 | [Send_Watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_watchdog) | host → driver | 5 | System |
| 23 | [Send_Respond_Temperature](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/status/#send_respond_temperature) | host → driver as a remote frame, driver → host as a data frame | 0 (remote) / 2 | Status requests |
| 24 | [Send_Respond_Voltage](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/status/#send_respond_voltage) | host → driver as a remote frame, driver → host as a data frame | 0 (remote) / 2 | Status requests |
| 25 | [Send_Respond_Device_Info](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/status/#send_respond_device_info) | host → driver as a remote frame, driver → host as a data frame | 0 (remote) / 7 | Status requests |
| 26 | [Send_Respond_State_of_Errors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/status/#send_respond_state_of_errors) | host → driver as a remote frame, driver → host as a data frame | 0 (remote) / 2 | Status requests |
| 30 | [Send_Heartbeat_Setup](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/#send_heartbeat_setup) | host → driver | 4 | System |
| 60 | [Respond_Gripper_data_pack](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/gripper/#respond_gripper_data_pack) | driver → host | 4 | Gripper |
| 61 | [Send_gripper_data_pack](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/gripper/#send_gripper_data_pack) | host → driver | 0, 5 | Gripper |
| 62 | [Send_gripper_calibrate](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/gripper/#send_gripper_calibrate) | host → driver | 0 | Gripper |

The driver's other messages (the motion commands, the gains and limits, the encoder and current requests) are
not listed here; they are in the [STEPFOC CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/reference/can/).

## By group

- [Gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/gripper/): the move command and its answer, the gripper calibration
- [System](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/system/): node ID, E-stop, idle, save, reset, clear, watchdog, heartbeat setup
- [Status requests](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can/status/): temperature, voltage, identity, the driver's error flags, the heartbeat

## The Python library

Every message the host can send has a method of the same name in `Spectral_BLDC.SpectralCAN`, listed in
[Python library](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/python/).

## Tools and downloads

[Build or decode a CAN frame, and download this firmware's JSON and DBC definitions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.1/reference/can-tools/).
